speaker: Petter Hörnfeldt
title: Ep16 - Interview with Petter Hoernfeldt - Mentour Pilot
question: In commercial aviation, why is an aviation psychologist suitability test so valuable before starting flight training?
guest: A suitability test with an aviation psychologist is something everyone hates doing and gets nervous about, but you have to do it because they can see parts of your personality that you might not be aware of. If there is something in there that will stop you from being successful in this profession—maybe you have a low tolerance to certain types of stress, or you cannot do several things at the same time at the rate that's needed—the only thing sadder than hearing that before you've started training is hearing it after you have paid 100,000 euros for your training. I recommend going to schools that require this, and if they don't, doing it yourself. If psychologists tell you you're suitable, you know you have what it takes even if you need to practice for entry exams; if not, you need someone to tell you before investing too much time and money.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
An aviation psychologist suitability test is valuable mainly because it predicts, before you commit large sums of money and years of your life, whether you are likely to succeed in training and in the job itself.

Commercial flight training often costs upwards of €100,000 or $100,000, and failing partway through leaves a trainee with debt and no licence. The assessment measures the things that are hard to teach and that strongly predict training outcomes: cognitive abilities such as spatial orientation, multitasking, memory, mental arithmetic and psychomotor coordination, plus personality traits such as stress tolerance, decision-making, teamwork, communication and conscientiousness.

This benefits everyone involved. Candidates get an objective, independent check on their aptitude and learn about weaknesses early. Flight schools and airlines get lower dropout rates and trainees who are more likely to pass type ratings and airline selection later. Safety benefits too, since most accidents involve human factors, so screening for sound judgment and crew cooperation matters.

It also aligns with regulation: after the Germanwings accident, EASA required airlines to psychologically assess pilots before line flying, so passing early reduces the risk of being rejected later.

models.answer:
Commercial flight training requires an enormous investment of time and money—often exceeding $100,000—making early validation of a candidate’s fitness essential before committing resources. Unlike standard medical exams or academic checks, an aviation psychologist suitability assessment evaluates the specific cognitive, psychomotor, and personality traits required on a modern flight deck. Through standardized testing and behavioral interviews, aviation psychologists measure spatial orientation, multitasking, working memory, stress resilience, emotional stability, and the interpersonal skills vital for effective Crew Resource Management and high-pressure decision-making. 

Identifying critical deficits beforehand protects both aspiring pilots and training organizations from costly mid-training washouts, while giving suitable candidates actionable feedback on trainable blind spots. Furthermore, because regulators such as EASA mandate psychological assessments before commercial line flying—and airlines use similar evaluations during recruitment—pre-training screening confirms that a student is not merely capable of earning a license, but is genuinely employable and psychologically suited for the long-term safety demands of an airline career.

noweb.answer: An aviation psychological suitability assessment is invaluable before flight training because it safeguards operational safety, career viability, and massive financial investment. Commercial pilot training frequently exceeds $100,000 and requires years of intense commitment, yet passing a medical exam and academic subjects does not guarantee cockpit aptitude. Aviation psychologists evaluate core cognitive and psychomotor capacities—such as spatial orientation, working memory, divided attention, and hand-eye coordination—alongside essential personality traits like emotional stability, stress tolerance, conscientiousness, and teamwork. Modern commercial flying relies heavily on Crew Resource Management, where clear communication, sound judgment under pressure, and balanced cockpit authority matter just as much as stick-and-rudder skill. Identifying cognitive bottlenecks, hazardous attitudes, or psychological vulnerabilities beforehand spares aspiring pilots from devastating mid-training washouts or failing airline selection boards after graduation. For sponsoring airlines and flight academies, early screening ensures training resources focus on candidates who can not only master aircraft handling, but operate safely and resiliently across a career in high-stakes, multi-crew environments.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
An aviation psychologist's suitability test is valuable mainly because flight training costs so much and so many trainees drop out. Getting an ATPL or MPL licence usually costs somewhere between €70,000 and €150,000, and trainees often pay it themselves or with loans. If you only find out partway through, or at an airline's selection stage, that you lack key aptitudes, you can lose a great deal of money and years of your life.

A professional assessment uses validated methods, much like those of DLR or airline selection centres. It measures the cognitive skills pilots need, such as spatial orientation, multitasking, short-term memory, mental arithmetic, attention and psychomotor coordination. It also looks at personality traits that matter for safety: how you handle stress, your decision-making, teamwork and crew resource management (CRM), and emotional stability.

The result gives you a realistic, independent view of your chances before you commit. If you have weaknesses that can be trained, it shows you what to work on before the real airline or flight school selection. For schools and airlines, screening candidates this way reduces dropout and the cost of failed training. It also supports the safety culture by catching unsuitable candidates early.

An aviation psychologist suitability test before starting commercial flight training is valuable because it objectively evaluates whether a candidate has the cognitive, psychomotor, and behavioral foundations required for a demanding cockpit career before committing substantial time and money. Commercial pilot training is expensive and intensive, and airlines rely on strict psychological selection standards; early assessment significantly reduces the risk of costly training failure or later rejection during airline hiring.

Specifically, these evaluations measure core aptitudes that are difficult to train—such as spatial orientation, multitasking, working memory, situational awareness, and sound decision-making under time pressure. Beyond technical aptitude, aviation psychologists assess personality traits, emotional resilience, stress tolerance, and interpersonal fit for Crew Resource Management, ensuring candidates can communicate effectively and stay composed during emergencies in a multi-crew environment. Finally, early screening helps identify potential psychological vulnerabilities or attitudes that could compromise flight safety or medical certification, allowing aspiring pilots to address gaps or make an informed career decision from the start.
